newsitem.title: BAHAMAS: Bahamas votes for new government on Friday.
newsitem.headline: Bahamas votes for new government on Friday.

text.p: Bahamians go to the polls on Friday, facing a choice of greater state involvement in the Caribbean nation's economy or going further down a market-driven road.

Almost 130,000 Bahamanians are registered to vote in a country where race is no longer an issue and significant progress has taken place in the last four-and-a-half years under reform-minded Prime Minister Hubert Ingraham, a 49-year-old lawyer.

Ingraham will lead his Free National Movement (FNM) into the election trying for a second term in office. The Progressive Liberal Party is seeking to recapture office following its defeat in 1992 for the first time in 25 years.

Since taking office in 1992, the Ingraham administration has implemented a major renovation of dilapidated schools, public buildings and docks. It has privatised money-draining hotels and attracted major new investment including names like Sun International, Disney and Hutchison International Port Holdings, a subsidiary of Hutchison Whampoa Ltd of Hong Kong.
Ingraham has worked hard to shed the Bahamas' reputation as a drug transit nation of corrupt politicians.
The state monopoly on broadcasting has been broken and the tourist industry in the Bahamian island of New Providence is thriving.
The problem of Haitian refugees is no longer a vexing issue, and state-owned Bahamasair is on target to reduce its annual losss of $20 million by half.

Ingraham has pledged that his government will continue on its course if relected, saying new investment was lined up. He says state-owned utility companies would be sold and he has promised full employment to all those who want to work.

On the campaign trail he made plenty of promises, as one Nassua columnist put it "throwing all propriety and fiscal resonsibilty to the winds, blatantly wooing all and sundry with outrageuos pre-election promises which even the Almighty himself would have a hard time fulfilling without bankrupting the Kingdom of Heaven."
On the downside, unemployment and the breakdown of family life have spawned problems among youths.

The biggest thorn for the government is crime, which came to a head in February with the murder of state minister for housing Charles Virgil -- the first person to be slain while in public office. There was no evidence to suggest that the murder was political but it shocked the nation.
During the PLP's 1970-79 watch, murders, burglaries and drugs offences soared and they have not abated under the FNM. The PLP says that if elected it would arm the police.
Much of the FNM's success is attributed to energy of Ingraham, who was fired as minister of housing in the former PLP government in 1984 after opposing corruption.
But a pay increase awarded to the civIl service two weeks before the election has sparked criticism.
The PLP is campaigning against the privatisation of state corporations and sticking to its ideology of state employment.
It says it will abolish real property tax on owner- occupied premises and reinstitute economic zones.
Sir Lynden Pindling, 67, says he will step down in early 1998, paving the way for a new leadership.

Pindling led the Bahamas to majority rule in 1967 and independence in 1973, and his policies helped to create a large black middle class. But his reputation has been badly tarnished by allegations of corruption.
